rv.q: At long last, a vampire musical that doesn't suck.
The good things about The Lost Boys are so good, in fact, that they make its fumbles especially frustrating; there's a sense of lost opportunity.

Co-writers David Hornsby (TV’s “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia”) and Chris Hoch improve the screenplay, tightening the original storyline, cutting some characters, upping the funny and giving the show more warmth.
The Lost Boys contains the finest spectacle I have seen this season outside of the Met Opera.
Ultimately, when this kind of scale manages to bring with it both genuine humor and beauty, I'm pulled toward enjoyment.

The Palace is a big venue of course and, for many hinterland punters, 'The Lost Boys' will deliver an epic Broadway blast, an amped-up escape from their prosaic realities and that will do it for a vampire musical.
Even if a few elements of this vampire love story remain a bit undercooked, it's definitely worth sinking your teeth into.
It's the best new musical on Broadway.
The Lost Boys, the Michael Arden-directed stage adaptation of the 1987 movie about teenage bloodsuckers, opens tonight at the Palace Theatre, and it's killer fun.
For director Michael Arden’s last hit, Maybe Happy Ending, he had the advantage of building a stunning staging out of a dramatically driven score and pitch-perfect book.
There is so much pleasure to be found in the atmospheric vampire elements that it may go by unnoticed.
The Lost Boys, starts with a bang and lives up to that adrenaline rush by delivering jaw-dropping sets and special effects.
The cumulative effect is undeniably exciting. Mainstream audiences will likely feel they are seeing an event.
The Lost Boys loiters in limbo between '80s nostalgia and uneven novelty.
The Lost Boys ultimately feels more redolent of a theme park attraction than theater.
I think it's better than the film, even with its flaws.
The Lost Boys doesn't know what it wants to be: a shocker, a tear-jerker or a parody.
For me, it was mostly lost time.

If anything, “The Lost Boys” is worse than all of them. It arrives at the tail end of what may be the weakest season for new musicals in decades, and any hope that it might redeem the season quickly disappears. The original film was never especially good, but it survives as a piece of 1980s kitschy teen fluff.
The Lost Boys delivers a gleefully propulsive blockbuster that breaks Broadway's vampire musical curse and gives a desperate season exactly what it needs.
The Lost Boys may be the most spectacular surprise of the Broadway season — a visually captivating show that actually improves on its source material.
I never expected to leave a musical about undead bloodsuckers thinking, 'That was kind of fun.'
While many audiences may have found what just they're looking for in 'The Lost Boys,' the musical still feels like a lost opportunity to be as good as it should be.

Review: The Lost Boys: The Musical at the Palace Theatre Palace Theatre ⋄ March 27, 2026-open-ended This vampire musical succeeds on spectacle, but belabors its themes. Loren Noveck LJ Benet, Ali Louis Bourzgui, and the company of The Lost Boys.

lo.t: Lottery opens the day before at 7:00 AM, closes at 2:00 PM the same day. Winners have 60 minutes to pay.
lo.inst: Limit 2 tickets per person. May be partial view.

ru.inst: Available on the day of the performance. Limit 2 tickets per person.

sg.ra: After the 2023 TSX lift the orchestra received wider seats and a slight rake, and center rows G-K are the unobstructed sweet spot before the mezzanine overhang begins at Row K per the official chart; AVFMS reports suggest the overhang only becomes visually noticeable closer to Row N-O, so center G-K is the cleanest post-reno picture.

sg.vl: Discount seats but mezz starts to bite
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang begins cutting in roughly at Orchestra Row K per the theatre's official seating chart, so rear-orchestra tickets (Row N onward) are priced well below center-premium but you give up the top of the proscenium; one AVFMS reviewer at Row N seat 119 still reported no overhang intrusion, so the rear orch is a real value play on non-spectacle shows that don't use high flying scenery.

Post-2023 lift reviewers specifically call out that the front-mezz sightline is 'incredible' and gives a panoramic view of the choreography, and multiple sources name center Rows A-C (or middle C-F) as the unobstructed sweet spot; avoid the first two side-aisle seats in Row A which Broadway Direct flags as obstructed by a safety railing that survived the renovation.

Unlike most Broadway houses, the Palace rear mezz sits on the same elevated tier rather than under a balcony overhang, so sightlines stay open to the top of the proscenium even at the back — a November 2025 AVFMS reviewer confirmed you are 'pretty high up but atleast you have a full view of the stage'; the tradeoff is distance plus the tight 1920s row spacing the reno preserved.

The Palace's mezz-level boxes are routinely sold as obstructed-view and nytix explicitly warns 'the box seats are not recommended, as they do not provide a clear view of the stage' — the severe side angle means upstage-left blocking is cut off; pick them only if you want the close-in vibe over actually seeing the full stage picture, and never for a dance-heavy or spectacle title.

The balcony survived the lift essentially unchanged — nytix flags that 'the view from the first row of the balcony may be blocked by a large horizontal bar, so sitting in the rows behind the first row is recommended,' and post-reno reviewers still call the balcony 'pretty far' from stage; there is no step-free access, so even the cheapest seat carries real friction.

vr.q: Tony Award for scenic design is over. The winner has been decided. There's no competition. There's nobody doing it like Lost Boys right now.

This is a show with really good bones, but if you can only go once, I would say maybe wait a couple weeks, wait for them to fine tune the things that they need to fine tune, and hopefully the final product lives up to that potential.
